briefing:
The Reserve Bank of India and MoSPI daily airfare intelligence pipeline records a headline Airfare Price Index (APIx) reading of 102.85 for the target run date of September 18, 2026, representing a 2.85% net increase over baseline medians. Upward price pressure was observed across all three monitored trunk corridors, led by the Calcutta–Bombay route with a Route-Level Index (RLI) of 104.34, followed by Delhi–Bombay at an RLI of 102.98, and Delhi–Bengaluru at an RLI of 101.19. The consolidated weighted price movement points to broad-based fare firming across the domestic aviation sector, driven predominantly by medium-term advance booking horizons rather than immediate spot market pressures.

A granular window-level decomposition reveals that the primary inflation driver across the aggregate index was the 30-day advance booking window ($T+30$), which carries a 20% weight in the APIx methodology. On the Calcutta–Bombay route, $T+30$ median fares exhibited a substantial relative price increase of 37.57%, escalating from a baseline median of ₹9,138 to a target median of ₹12,571. Similarly, Delhi–Bombay registered systematic upward re-pricing across its $T+30$ and $T+45$ horizons, both reaching ₹7,019 against baseline medians of ₹6,530 and ₹6,684, respectively. On the Delhi–Bengaluru route, $T+30$ fares increased by 13.27% (moving from ₹8,829 to ₹10,001), though the corridor's aggregate gain was partially tempered by near-term price softening in the $T+1$ (-8.39%) and $T+15$ (-5.47%) departure windows.

The full scraped market dataset uncovers notable structural price dispersion and airport-specific fare anomalies across carriers. On the Delhi–Bombay corridor at $T+7$, secondary hub departures out of Noida International Airport in Jewar (DXN) introduced significant downward price variance, exemplified by Akasa Air flight QP-1940 priced at ₹4,860—markedly below the primary Indira Gandhi International Airport (DEL) route median of ₹6,530. Secondary carriers and alternative hub routings via Ghaziabad/Hindon (HDO) and Navi Mumbai (NMI) consistently defined the lower boundary of fare distributions. Conversely, the sharp spike observed on Calcutta–Bombay at $T+30$ reflects pronounced capacity tightening on direct non-stop flights operated by major carriers, where IndiGo direct services ranged between ₹13,155 and ₹15,150, forcing the median standard fare significantly upward despite lower-priced multi-stop options remaining available.

From a monetary policy and statistical perspective, the 2.85% uplift in domestic airfares indicates emerging upside risk within the transport and communication subgroup of the Consumer Price Index (CPI) for October 2026 travel dates. The concentration of price increases in the 30-day advance window strongly points to heightened forward demand matching seasonal holiday travel periods. While near-term ($T+1$) spot market stability and secondary airport capacity expansion provide modest buffers against immediate inflation pass-through, policy makers should continue monitoring core service inflation metrics for persistence. Supply-side developments—particularly carrier fleet deployment and fare segmentation across emerging metro satellite airports—will remain critical factors in determining whether these airfare increases represent a transitory seasonal adjustment or a broader firming in domestic service demand.
